### # Traditional Spark Architecture 

Traditionally Spark architecture was **tightly coupled**: the driver, user code, and execution engine all lived in a very connected environment

The **SparkContext** was the original entry point to this system and acted as the connection between the application and the cluster. It was created inside the driver and was responsible for establishing communication with the cluster manager and initializing the resources needed for execution.

The **driver** sat inside the cluster network and constantly handled execution-level communication, where every DataFrame transformation, shuffle, or query plan required back-and-forth messaging between the driver and executors.

As workloads scaled, the driver became a **bottleneck** because it had to maintain DAGs, task schedules, and execution metadata in memory, increasing CPU and RAM usage on a single coordination point and limiting scalability in large workloads.

Since the driver was part of the execution environment, scaling or upgrading was not independent. Spark versions, Python libraries, and dependencies had to stay aligned across client and cluster, and local environments often had to mirror the cluster, increasing setup overhead and reducing flexibility.

![[Pasted image 20260525023956.png]]
### # Apache Spark 4.0

In Apache Spark 4.0, the architecture shifts to a **decoupled client-server model using Spark Connect**, where the SparkSession runs as a lightweight client outside the cluster.
#### # Spark Connect API

Spark-Connect API is a [gRPC](https://grpc.io) based API that runs as a server to connect spark client applications with the spark driver and cluster

![[Pasted image 20260522234801.png]]

> The driver is no more part of the client
> Spark now ships a separate client library which wraps the spark-connect API. 
> This makes sure that spark client applications do not need full installation and dependency of the spark. 
#### # DataFrame as the Intermediate Protocol

Spark continues to expose the same DataFrame and Dataset APIs, but internally these operations are converted into logical plans and then gRPC calls sent to the remote Spark server for execution.

![[Pasted image 20260525022934.png]]

### # Spark Applications

Spark Applications consist of a **driver process** and a set of **executor processes**. 
#### # Driver 

The driver process runs your main() function, sits on a node in the cluster, and is responsible for three things: 

- maintaining information about the Spark Application
- responding to a user’s program or input
- analyzing, distributing, and scheduling work across the executors (discussed momentarily). 

The driver process is absolutely essential—it’s the heart of a Spark Application and maintains all relevant information during the lifetime of the application.
##### # SparkSession

Spark Application is accessed  through a **driver process** called the SparkSession. 
The SparkSession instance is the way Spark executes user-defined manipulations across the cluster. There is a one-to-one correspondence between a SparkSession and a Spark Application.

> **SparkSession** is the modern replacement of **SparkContext**
#### # Executors

The executors are responsible for actually carrying out the work that the driver assigns them. This means that each executor is responsible for only two things: 

- executing code assigned to it by the driver
- reporting the state of the computation on that executor back to the driver node.

![[Pasted image 20260522205652.png]]
#### # Cluster manager

The cluster manager controls physical machines and allocates resources to Spark Applications. This can be one of three core cluster managers: Spark’s standalone cluster manager, YARN, or Mesos. This means that there can be multiple Spark Applications running on a cluster at the same time.

We can look at it this way 

- Spark employs a cluster manager that keeps track of the resources available.
- The driver process is responsible for executing the driver program’s commands across the executors to complete a given task.

#### # Spark’s Language APIs

For the most part, Spark presents some core “concepts” in every language; these concepts are then translated into Spark code that runs on the cluster of machines. If you use just the Structured APIs, you can expect all languages to have similar performance characteristics. 

![[Pasted image 20260522205937.png]]

There is a SparkSession object available to the user, which is the entrance point to running Spark code. When using Spark from Python or R, you don’t write explicit JVM instructions; instead, you write Python and R code that Spark translates into code that it then can run on the executor JVMs.

### # Spark Applications Flow

#### # Application hierarchy 

- At the top of the hierarchy is the **Spark Application itself**, which represents the full program submitted by the user:  logic, configuration, and execution flow for a single workload.
- Inside the application sits the **driver process**, which acts as the central coordinator.
	- Within the driver, the **SparkSession** is teh userfacing entry point. It is created inside the driver and provides the interface through which user code interacts with Spark.
- Once the execution plan is created, the driver communicates with the **cluster manager**, which is responsible for resource allocation (It does not execute any computation itself but assigns CPU, memory, and worker nodes to the Spark Application).
- Below the cluster manager are the **executors**, which run on worker nodes. Executors are responsible for executing tasks assigned by the driver and returning results. They also store intermediate data when needed, such as cached partitions or shuffle outputs.
- At the lowest level are **tasks**, which are the smallest unit of execution in Spark. Each task operates on a single partition of data, and multiple tasks are executed in parallel across executors to complete a stage.

**![](data:image/png;base64,)**
#### The driver

Everything in the application flows downward from the Driver. A Driver is just a JVM process. Where the Driver lives depends on how you launch the job. 
- _In client mode_, it stays on your laptop or submission machine, orchestrating everything remotely. 
- _In cluster mode_, it moves into the cluster itself, running on a dedicated node. 

We define transformations, the Driver incrementally assembles them into a **logical DAG** of operations. No actual computation happens until you call an action.At that point, the Driver turns the logical DAG into a **physical execution plan** and starts running tasks on executors.

![[Pasted image 20260525023509.png]]

The Driver cuts the DAG into **stages**
Each stage is then broken into **tasks**, one per data partition. These tasks are the actual work units that will eventually land on executors somewhere in the cluster.
#### The driver as a Scheduler

Once the tasks exist, the Driver takes on the role of a scheduler. It talks to the Cluster Resource Manager to request resources, hands batches of tasks to available executors, and keeps a close eye on their progress. If an executor dies, the Driver knows which tasks were running there and can resubmit them elsewhere. 

At the same time, the Driver keeps lineage information for [[RDDs(Resiliant Distributed Dataset)]] and partitions, maintains the logical-to-physical mapping of operations, and exposes this through the Spark UI.

![[Pasted image 20260525032839.png]]
#### # DAGScheduler

The DAGScheduler uses the logical plan and break it into **stages**. A stage can run as long as its input partitions are available locally. The DAGScheduler's job is to translate logical operations into **stage boundaries**. It looks at your **RDD lineage**, identifies wide dependencies like `groupByKey` or `join`, and decides where data shuffles must occur. Every shuffle creates a stage boundary because data has to move between nodes.

![[Pasted image 20260525032411.png]]

From there, the DAGScheduler breaks each stage into a set of tasks called **TaskSets**, one per partition, and sends them to the **TaskScheduler**. 

>DAGScheduler also tracks their lineage; to recompute lost partitions in case of failure instead of starting your job from scratch.

DAGScheduler is also the one who decides job success or failure. If a stage can't make progress after repeated attempts (for example due to corrupted input data) it declares the job to have failed.

It is important to note that, the DAGScheduler makes _dynamic_ decisions. It doesn't pre-schedule all stages at once. Instead, it reacts to stage completions and unlocks child stages on-the-fly.
#### # TaskScheduler

Once the DAGScheduler has carved the DAG into stages and handed off a TaskSet for the next stage, the **TaskScheduler**. This is the part of Spark that stops thinking in lineage and starts thinking in terms of machines and slots.

The TaskScheduler doesn't care about RDDs or shuffles. Its job is mechanical:

- Take each TaskSet from the DAGScheduler
- Work with the SchedulerBackend to request executors and figure out where tasks can run
- Assign tasks to executors, trying to keep them close to their data (see below) whenever possible.
- Retry failed tasks when necessary

If an executor dies or a task throws an exception, the TaskScheduler resubmits the task to another executor

>This handoff — DAGScheduler to TaskScheduler — is what converts a _logical_ plan into a _physical_ reality running across the cluster. Where the DAGScheduler thinks in stages, the TaskScheduler works in terms of executors and available CPU cores — the slots where tasks will run.

TaskScheduler itself does not launch tasks. It hands them to the SchedulerBackend.
#### # SchedulerBackend

The **SchedulerBackend** is the messenger between Spark and the cluster manager. Its responsibilities include:

- Talking to the cluster manager to request new executors
- Launching and killing executors as needed
- Reporting executor availability back to the TaskScheduler

When you see Spark dynamically scale executors up and down during a job, that's the SchedulerBackend negotiating with the cluster manager behind the scenes.
#### # BlockManagerMaster

Spark processes everything as partitions, and each partition becomes a **block** stored either in memory or on disk. And every RDD partition, every shuffle file, every broadcast variable goes through the BlockManager. When an executor needs a block of data, the BlockManager either hands it over locally or fetches it from a neighbor.

> When a wide transformation like `reduceByKey` runs, tasks often need to fetch intermediate data (shuffle blocks) produced by other tasks on different executors. The BlockManager handles these lookups and transfers. The same mechanism is also used when tasks fetch cached RDDs or broadcast variables from remote nodes. If data isn't local, the BlockManager finds it, and how to pull it across the network.

Every executor has its own BlockManager, but the Driver hosts the **BlockManagerMaster**, which keeps a global map of all block locations across the cluster. Whenever a task needs a block, the BlockManager can serve it directly if it's local, or fetch it from a remote executor if necessary. This is the mechanism that makes shuffles, caching, and recomputation possible.

BlockManager handles:

- Storage and retrieval of blocks in memory or on disk
- Replication for fault tolerance, so losing one executor doesn't mean losing the only copy of a partition
- Data exchange between executors during shuffles or when fetching cached partitions
